claim: More than 30% of genes in higher eukaryotes are regulated by promoter-proximal pausing of RNA polymerase II (Pol II).
source: More than 30% of genes in higher eukaryotes are regulated by promoter-proximal pausing of RNA polymerase II (Pol II).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to published literature (Core et al., 2008; Nechaev et al., 2010; Min et al., 2011) as referenced in the Introduction section.

claim: Phosphorylation of Pol II CTD by positive transcription elongation factor b (P-TEFb) is a necessary precursor event that enables productive transcription elongation.
source: Phosphorylation of Pol II CTD by positive transcription elongation factor b (P-TEFb) is a necessary precursor event that enables productive transcription elongation.
evidence: This claim is supported by established scientific knowledge about transcription regulation.

claim: MePCE is a core component of the 7SK snRNP complex.
source: In this report, we utilize mouse and human models to reveal methylphosphate capping enzyme (MePCE), a core component of the 7SK snRNP complex, as the cognate substrate for Jumonji domain-containing 6 (JMJD6)'s novel proteolytic function.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to published literature (Jeronimo et al., 2007; Xue et al., 2010) in the Introduction.

claim: JMJD6 cleaves MePCE.
source: In this report, we utilize mouse and human models to reveal methylphosphate capping enzyme (MePCE), a core component of the 7SK snRNP complex, as the cognate substrate for Jumonji domain-containing 6 (JMJD6)'s novel proteolytic function.
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple experimental data including enzymatic assays in vivo and in vitro, binding assays, and crystal structure analysis presented in the manuscript.

claim: Four out of eight JMJD6 molecules within an asymmetric unit bound to monomethylarginine.
source: Interestingly, four out of eight JMJD6 molecules within an asymmetric unit bound to monomethylarginine, which coordinates with Fe2+ and alpha-KG in the catalytic center similar to that of JMJD5 and methylarginines (Figure 1, Figure 1—figure supplements 1–3, Supplementary file 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by crystallographic data presented in Figure 1 and supplementary figures.

claim: The catalytic center of JMJD6 contains a negatively charged microenvironment.
source: On the other hand, the structure of the catalytic core of JMJD6 shows some critical similarity to those of JMJD5 and JMJD7, with a negatively charged microenvironment near the catalytic center (Hong et al., 2010; Liu et al., 2018), suggesting positively charged substrates (Figure 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by structural data from the crystal structure shown in Figure 1 and cited literature.

claim: The methyl group of methylarginine is far away from either the divalent ion or alpha-KG in the JMJD6 catalytic center.
source: Second, the methyl group is far away from either the divalent ion or alpha-KG, suggesting JMJD6 may not act as lysine or arginine demethylases to remove methyl groups on the sidechain of either lysine or arginine.
evidence: This claim is based on structural observations from the crystal structure analysis.

claim: JMJD6 may not act as lysine or arginine demethylases.
source: Second, the methyl group is far away from either the divalent ion or alpha-KG, suggesting JMJD6 may not act as lysine or arginine demethylases to remove methyl groups on the sidechain of either lysine or arginine.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the structural data showing the position of the methyl group relative to catalytic residues.

claim: Commercially available protease inhibitor cocktail (Roche) at 2x concentration cannot inhibit activities of JMJD5, JMJD6, and JMJD7.
source: This novelty is particularly exemplified by the fact that commercially available protease inhibitor cocktail (Roche) at 2x concentration cannot inhibit activities of JMJD5, JMJD6, and JMJD7.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental observations regarding the novel catalytic mechanism of these enzymes.

claim: Mass spectrometry analysis of purified recombinant JMJD6 samples could not detect any protease contaminants.
source: Furthermore, a comprehensive protein composition analysis using mass spectrometry (Supplementary file 2) of all purified recombinant JMJD6 samples used in the following experiments could not detect any protease contaminants.
evidence: This claim is supported by mass spectrometry data presented in Supplementary file 2.

claim: All protein components of the 7SK snRNP complex including MEPCE, LARP7, and HEXIM1 are drastically decreased in MEF cells without Jmjd6.
source: Interestingly, all protein components of the 7SK snRNP complex including MEPCE, LARP7, and HEXIM1 are drastically decreased in the MEF cells without Jmjd6 (Figure 2A).
evidence: This claim is supported by Western blot data shown in Figure 2A.

claim: RNA-Seq data does not support direct transcriptional downregulation of 7SK snRNP complex members at mRNA level.
source: However, our RNA-Seq data does not support direct transcriptional downregulation of 7SK snRNP complex members at mRNA level (Supplementary file 3). All of them, including MePCE, LARP7, and HEXIM1 have similar mRNA levels with or without Jmjd6.
evidence: This claim is supported by RNA-Seq data presented in Supplementary file 3.

claim: When JMJD6 is overexpressed in Jmjd6 knockout MEF cells, protein levels of LARP7 and HEXIM1 are rescued, whereas MePCE is undetectable or significantly reduced.
source: However, when we introduce back JMJD6 via overexpression into MEF cells lacking Jmjd6, protein levels of LARP7 and HEXIM1 are rescued, whereas MePCE is undetectable (Figure 2A) or significantly reduced (Figure 2—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: This claim is supported by Western blot data shown in Figure 2A and Figure 2—figure supplement 1C.

claim: A lower molecular weight form of MePCE appears in wild-type MEF and wild-type JMJD6 overexpression in Jmjd6 knockout MEF, but not in Jmjd6 knockout MEF or inactive mutant JMJD6 overexpression in Jmjd6 knockout MEF.
source: Our hypothesis was vindicated with the emergence of a lower molecular weight form of MePCE in wild-type MEF and wild-type JMJD6 overexpression in Jmjd6 knockout MEF, whereas the lower molecular weight form of MePCE was not detectable in the Jmjd6 knockout MEF, and inactive mutant JMJD6 overexpression in Jmjd6 knockout MEF (Figure 2B).
evidence: This claim is supported by Western blot data shown in Figure 2B.

claim: JMJD6 cleaves MePCE in vitro.
source: Consistent with our in vivo results, JMJD6 cleaves MePCE in vitro (Figure 2C,D), but not HEXIM1, HEXIM2, nor LARP7 (data not shown).
evidence: This claim is supported by in vitro enzymatic assay data shown in Figure 2C and 2D.

claim: JMJD6 does not cleave HEXIM1, HEXIM2, or LARP7 in vitro.
source: Consistent with our in vivo results, JMJD6 cleaves MePCE in vitro (Figure 2C,D), but not HEXIM1, HEXIM2, nor LARP7 (data not shown).
evidence: This claim is supported by in vitro enzymatic assay data (mentioned but not shown).

claim: Upon cleavage of MePCE by JMJD6 in vitro, a band with molecular weight ~25 kDa was detected by antibody against His6-tag at the N-terminal.
source: Upon cleavage of MePCE by JMJD6 in vitro, a band with molecular weight ~25 kDa was detected by antibody against His6-tag at the N-terminal (Figure 2C).
evidence: This claim is supported by Western blot data shown in Figure 2C.

claim: MePCE contains a total of 689 residues and a theoretical molecular weight of 74.4 kDa.
source: To provide context, MePCE contains a total of 689 residues and a theoretical molecular weight of 74.4 kDa, whereas it is detected at ~90 kDa on SDS-PAGE gel due to its high content of proline residues (10.7%).
evidence: This claim is based on the known sequence of MePCE.

claim: MePCE is detected at ~90 kDa on SDS-PAGE gel due to its high content of proline residues (10.7%).
source: To provide context, MePCE contains a total of 689 residues and a theoretical molecular weight of 74.4 kDa, whereas it is detected at ~90 kDa on SDS-PAGE gel due to its high content of proline residues (10.7%).
evidence: This claim is based on experimental observation and inference about the effect of proline content on protein migration.

claim: Dominant peaks corresponding to cleaved MePCE peptide products were detected by mass spectrometry when MePCE (161-179) R171-me2s/C177S peptide was incubated with JMJD6, but not with peptide alone or with inactive mutant JMJD6.
source: In line with our expectations, dominant peaks corresponding to the cleaved MePCE peptide products were detected by mass spectrometry, but not in either peptide alone or with an inactive mutant version of JMJD6 (Figure 2E).
evidence: This claim is supported by mass spectrometry data shown in Figure 2E.

claim: The highest binding affinity between JMJD6 and MePCE peptides was exhibited by MePCE (154-184)-R171-me2s peptide with Kd = 159 ± 77 nM.
source: The highest binding affinity was exhibited by the MePCE (154-184)-R171-me2s peptide with Kd = 159 ± 77 nM, followed by the peptide containing no modification with Kd = 471 ± 292 nM, and lastly the peptide with R170-me2s with Kd = 568 ± 316 nM.
evidence: This claim is supported by Microscale Thermophoresis (MST) assay data shown in Figure 3C.

claim: Methylation on R171 of MePCE enhances binding to JMJD6 nearly 3-fold compared to no modification.
source: These data suggest that methylation on R171 enhances binding nearly 3-fold compared to no modification, whereas methylation on R170 diminishes binding marginally.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the binding affinity measurements obtained via MST.

claim: The YASARA Energy Minimization Server yielded a theoretical model that positions R171 in the identical position to the monomethyl-arginine observed in the crystal model.
source: Interestingly, the YASARA Energy Minimization Server developed by Dr. Kevin Karplus' group yielded a theoretical model that positions R171 in the identical position to the monomethyl-arginine observed in our crystal model (Figure 3—figure supplement 2A; Krieger et al., 2009).
evidence: This claim is supported by computational modeling data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 2A.

claim: The energy-minimized model displayed eight separate charge-charge interactions between JMJD6 and MePCE.
source: Furthermore, the energy-minimized model displayed eight separate charge-charge interactions between JMJD6 and MePCE (Figure 3G).
evidence: This claim is supported by computational modeling data shown in Figure 3G.

claim: JMJD6 exhibits low binding affinity to Histone 3 peptides with Kd = 77 ± 34 μM for H3 peptide and Kd = 98 ± 14 μM for H3R2me2s peptide.
source: For the Histone three peptides, low binding affinity was exhibited with Kd = 77 ± 34 μM for H3 peptide and Kd = 98 ± 14 μM for H3R2me2s peptide.
evidence: This claim is supported by MST assay data shown in Figure 3D and 3E.

claim: Wild-type MePCE generates two bands when probed with anti-His6 antibody in a western blot, whereas mutant MePCE (with -RRRR- replaced to -AAAA- at the cleavage site) does not.
source: Interestingly, when probed with anti-His6 antibody in a western blot, wild-type MePCE generates two bands of MePCE (Figure 3I, left lane), consistent with Figure 2B, whereas the mutant version does not (Figure 3I, right lane), suggesting that this site is the authentic cleavage site for JMJD6.
evidence: This claim is supported by Western blot data shown in Figure 3I.

claim: Ser2p-CTD of Pol II is drastically reduced (~80%) in MEF cells without Jmjd6.
source: Consistent with all our current and previous findings, Ser2p-CTD of Pol II is drastically reduced (~80%) in MEF cells without Jmjd6, despite CDK9 levels remaining unchanged, suggesting that Ser2p-CTD of Pol II is regulated by JMJD6 (Figure 4A,B).
evidence: This claim is supported by Western blot data shown in Figure 4A and quantification in Figure 4B.

claim: CDK9 levels remain unchanged in MEF cells without Jmjd6.
source: Consistent with all our current and previous findings, Ser2p-CTD of Pol II is drastically reduced (~80%) in MEF cells without Jmjd6, despite CDK9 levels remaining unchanged, suggesting that Ser2p-CTD of Pol II is regulated by JMJD6 (Figure 4A,B).
evidence: This claim is supported by Western blot data shown in Figure 4A.

claim: Pol II Ser2p-CTD is dramatically increased in 293T cells with MePCE knockout compared to wild-type.
source: To our great satisfaction, Pol II Ser2p-CTD is dramatically increased in 293 T cells with MePCE knockout (Figure 4C, right lane) compared to the wild-type (Figure 4C, left lane).
evidence: This claim is supported by Western blot data shown in Figure 4C.

claim: The content of Ser2p-CTD of Pol II is recovered when JMJD6 is re-expressed in Jmjd6 knockout MEF cells.
source: The content of Ser2p-CTD of Pol II is recovered when JMJD6 is re-expressed (Figure 4A,B), suggesting the direct relation of JMJD6 and phosphorylation of Ser2-CTD of Pol II in vivo.
evidence: This claim is supported by Western blot data shown in Figure 4A and quantification in Figure 4B.

claim: JMJD6 exhibits strong binding affinity to nonspecific ssRNA.
source: When these results are aggregated with previously published reports, whereby (1) JMJD6 exhibits strong binding affinity to nonspecific ssRNA as we previously reported (Figure 4D; Hong et al., 2010)
evidence: This claim is supported by previously published data (Hong et al., 2010).

claim: JMJD6 associates with BRD4.
source: (2) JMJD6 associates with BRD4 as reported by others (Figure 4D; Rahman et al., 2011; Konuma et al., 2017)
evidence: This claim is supported by previously published data (Rahman et al., 2011; Konuma et al., 2017).

claim: 7SK snRNP complex pulled-down through HEXIM1 antibody from HEK293 cells could be disrupted by JMJD6 in vitro, as indicated by the decrease in CDK9 levels.
source: Here, our observation regarding the direct relation of JMJD6 and level of Ser2p-CTD of Pol II in vivo is corroborated by Liu et al.'s report, in which 7SK snRNP complex pulled-down through HEXIM1 antibody from HEK293 cells could be disrupted by JMJD6 in vitro, as indicated by the decrease in CDK9 levels (Liu et al., 2013)
evidence: This claim is supported by previously published data (Liu et al., 2013).

claim: JMJD6 is specifically associated with BRD4 through the ET domain.
source: First, JMJD6 is specifically associated with BRD4 through the ET domain (Rahman et al., 2011; Konuma et al., 2017)
evidence: This claim is supported by previously published data (Rahman et al., 2011; Konuma et al., 2017).

claim: BRD4 is very well established to recruit P-TEFb to paused Pol II.
source: while BRD4 is very well established to recruit P-TEFb to paused Pol II (Yang et al., 2005; Yang et al., 2008).
evidence: This claim is supported by previously published data (Yang et al., 2005; Yang et al., 2008).

claim: JMJD5 and JMJD7 are proteases.
source: The findings that JMJD5 and JMJD7 are in fact proteases was highly unexpected, and required multiple lines of evidence pursued with great scrutiny.
evidence: This claim is supported by previously published data from the authors' group (Liu et al., 2017; Liu et al., 2018).

claim: JMJD5 and JMJD7 cleave after methylated arginine.
source: In this report, the novel protease activity of JMJD6, which cleaves before the methylated arginine, is remarkably distinct to the cleavage after the methylated arginine mediated by JMJD5 and JMJD7 (Liu et al., 2017; Liu et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by previously published data (Liu et al., 2017; Liu et al., 2018).

claim: JMJD6 cleaves before methylated arginine.
source: In this report, the novel protease activity of JMJD6, which cleaves before the methylated arginine, is remarkably distinct to the cleavage after the methylated arginine mediated by JMJD5 and JMJD7 (Liu et al., 2017; Liu et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data presented in the manuscript, particularly the mass spectrometry data in Figure 2E.

claim: JMJD6 knockout in mice results in neonatal lethality.
source: The totality of our results is consistent with the critical role of JMJD6 in embryonic development, which is neonatal lethal without Jmjd6 (Li et al., 2003; Böse et al., 2004).
evidence: This claim is supported by previously published data (Li et al., 2003; Böse et al., 2004).

claim: Growth of MEF cells without Jmjd6 is severely compromised.
source: It explains why growth of MEF cells without Jmjd6 is severely compromised, similar to those without either Jmjd5 or Jmjd7 (Liu et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental observations and comparison to previously published data (Liu et al., 2017).

claim: In higher eukaryotes, over ~30% genes are regulated by Pol II promoter-proximal pausing.
source: In higher eukaryotes, over ~30% genes are regulated by Pol II promoter-proximal pausing (Core et al., 2008; Nechaev et al., 2010; Min et al., 2011)
evidence: This claim is supported by previously published data (Core et al., 2008; Nechaev et al., 2010; Min et al., 2011).

claim: Pol II promoter-proximal pausing is resultant from nucleosome barriers at +1 position of transcription start sites.
source: In higher eukaryotes, over ~30% genes are regulated by Pol II promoter-proximal pausing (Core et al., 2008; Nechaev et al., 2010; Min et al., 2011), which is resultant from nucleosome barriers at +1 position of transcription start sites (Weber et al., 2014; Voong et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by previously published data (Weber et al., 2014; Voong et al., 2016).

claim: JMJD5 and JMJD7 specifically cleave histone tails and potentially generate tailless nucleosomes.
source: We recently discovered that a group of JmjC domain containing protein family including JMJD5 and JMJD7 specifically cleave histone tails and potentially generate tailless nucleosomes.
evidence: This claim is supported by previously published data from the authors' group (Liu et al., 2017; Liu et al., 2018).

claim: The cleavage activity by JMJD5 and JMJD7 could be associated with the release of the promoter-proximal paused Pol II and may trigger Pol II into productive elongation in higher eukaryotes.
source: The cleavage activity by JMJD5 and JMJD7 could be associated with the release of the promoter-proximal paused Pol II and may trigger Pol II into productive elongation in higher eukaryotes, such as mouse and human (Liu et al., 2017; Liu et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is speculative and based on previously published data (Liu et al., 2017; Liu et al., 2018).

claim: The cleavage activity of JMJD5 on histone tails was independently reported by another group.
source: The cleavage activity of JMJD5 on histone tails was also independently reported by another group (Shen et al., 2017), thus cross-validating our respective discoveries.
evidence: This claim is supported by previously published data (Shen et al., 2017).

claim: The binding affinity between BRD4 and P-TEFb is ~0.5 μM.
source: However, the binding affinity between BRD4 and P-TEFb (~0.5 μM) (Itzen et al., 2014) is much weaker than that that of TAT and P-TEFb (~3 nM) (Wei et al., 1998; Tahirov et al., 2010; Schulze-Gahmen et al., 2014)
evidence: This claim is supported by previously published data (Itzen et al., 2014).

claim: The binding affinity between TAT and P-TEFb is ~3 nM.
source: However, the binding affinity between BRD4 and P-TEFb (~0.5 μM) (Itzen et al., 2014) is much weaker than that that of TAT and P-TEFb (~3 nM) (Wei et al., 1998; Tahirov et al., 2010; Schulze-Gahmen et al., 2014)
evidence: This claim is supported by previously published data (Wei et al., 1998; Tahirov et al., 2010; Schulze-Gahmen et al., 2014).

claim: BRD4 lacks a RNA binding motif.
source: and BRD4 lacks a RNA binding motif (Wu and Chiang, 2007).
evidence: This claim is supported by previously published data (Wu and Chiang, 2007).

claim: JMJD6 nonspecifically binds to single stranded RNA with high affinity (~40 nM).
source: Incidentally, we found that JMJD6 nonspecifically binds to single stranded RNA with high affinity (~40 nM) (Hong et al., 2010).
evidence: This claim is supported by previously published data from the authors' group (Hong et al., 2010).

claim: JMJD6 was first cloned as phosphatidylserine (PS) receptor.
source: It was first cloned as phosphatidylserine (PS) receptor (Fadok et al., 2000), but was corrected as a nucleus expressed protein unrelated to PS (Böse et al., 2004; Cikala et al., 2004; Cui et al., 2004).
evidence: This claim is supported by previously published data (Fadok et al., 2000).

claim: JMJD6 was corrected as a nucleus expressed protein unrelated to PS.
source: It was first cloned as phosphatidylserine (PS) receptor (Fadok et al., 2000), but was corrected as a nucleus expressed protein unrelated to PS (Böse et al., 2004; Cikala et al., 2004; Cui et al., 2004).
evidence: This claim is supported by previously published data (Böse et al., 2004; Cikala et al., 2004; Cui et al., 2004).

claim: JMJD6 was reported to contain arginine demethylase activity on histone tails.
source: It was later reported to contain arginine demethylase activity on histone tails (Chang et al., 2007)
evidence: This claim is supported by previously published data (Chang et al., 2007).

claim: JMJD6 was reported to have hydroxylase activity on splicing factor U2AF65.
source: hydroxylase activity on splicing factor U2AF65 (Webby et al., 2009)
evidence: This claim is supported by previously published data (Webby et al., 2009).

claim: JMJD6 was reported to have hydroxylase activity on histone tails.
source: and histone tails (Han et al., 2012)
evidence: This claim is supported by previously published data (Han et al., 2012).

claim: JMJD6 was reported to have both arginine demethylase activities on histone tails and RNA demethylase activities on 5' prime of 7SK snRNA.
source: and both arginine demethylase activities on histone tails and RNA demethylase activities on 5' prime of 7SK snRNA (Liu et al., 2013)
evidence: This claim is supported by previously published data (Liu et al., 2013).

claim: JMJD6 was reported to have PS binding activity.
source: and surprisingly PS binding (Neumann et al., 2015; Yang et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by previously published data (Neumann et al., 2015; Yang et al., 2015).

claim: MePCE was first characterized as a component of the 7SK snRNP complex which acts as a capping enzyme on the gamma phosphate at the 5'end of 7SK RNA.
source: MePCE (methylphosphate capping enzyme) was first characterized as a component of the 7SK snRNP complex which acts as a capping enzyme on the gamma phosphate at the 5'end of 7SK RNA (Jeronimo et al., 2007).
evidence: This claim is supported by previously published data (Jeronimo et al., 2007).

claim: A capping-independent function of MePCE via stabilization of 7SK snRNA and facilitation in the assembly of 7SK snRNP was reported.
source: Furthermore, a capping-independent function of MePCE via stabilization of 7SK snRNA and facilitation in the assembly of 7SK snRNP was reported by Dr. Qiang Zhou's group (Xue et al., 2010).
evidence: This claim is supported by previously published data (Xue et al., 2010).

claim: Knockdown of MePCE led to destabilization of the 7SK snRNP complex in vivo.
source: Knockdown of MePCE led to destabilization of the 7SK snRNP complex in vivo (Xue et al., 2010; Singh et al., 2011; C Quaresma et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by previously published data (Xue et al., 2010; Singh et al., 2011; C Quaresma et al., 2016).

claim: A nonsense variant of MePCE is reported to be associated with a neurodevelopmental disorder exhibiting hyperphosphorylation of Pol II, potentially caused by enhanced activation of CDK9 complex.
source: A nonsense variant of MePCE is reported to be associated with a neurodevelopmental disorder exhibiting hyperphosphorylation of Pol II, potentially caused by enhanced activation of CDK9 complex (Schneeberger et al., 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by previously published data (Schneeberger et al., 2019).

claim: MePCE may work in an 7SK snRNP independent manner to recruit CDK9 on a small group of genes.
source: Interestingly, one report showed that MePCE may also work in an 7SK snRNP independent manner to recruit CDK9 on a small group of genes (Shelton et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by previously published data (Shelton et al., 2018).

claim: JMJD6 barely binds to ssRNA without the C-terminal flexible region.
source: However, truncation analysis showed that JMJD6 barely binds to ssRNA without the C-terminal flexible region (Hong et al., 2010).
evidence: This claim is supported by previously published data from the authors' group (Hong et al., 2010).

claim: The C-terminal domain of JMJD6 may serve as ssRNA binding motif.
source: This suggests that the C-terminal domain of JMJD6 may just serve as ssRNA binding motif and RNAs are not a substrate for the enzymatic activity of JMJD6.
evidence: This claim is inferred from truncation analysis data.

claim: RNAs are not a substrate for the enzymatic activity of JMJD6.
source: This suggests that the C-terminal domain of JMJD6 may just serve as ssRNA binding motif and RNAs are not a substrate for the enzymatic activity of JMJD6.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the observation that the C-terminal domain is required for RNA binding but not for catalytic activity.

claim: JMJD5 recognizes methylarginines via a Tudor-domain-like structure near the catalytic center.
source: As we reported, JMJD5 and JMJD7 specifically recognize methylarginines of histone tails via a Tudor-domain-like structure near the catalytic center of JMJD5, which could specifically recognize methylarginines, but not methyllysine (Liu et al., 2017; Liu et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by previously published data from the authors' group (Liu et al., 2017; Liu et al., 2018).

claim: JMJD5 could specifically recognize methylarginines, but not methyllysine.
source: As we reported, JMJD5 and JMJD7 specifically recognize methylarginines of histone tails via a Tudor-domain-like structure near the catalytic center of JMJD5, which could specifically recognize methylarginines, but not methyllysine (Liu et al., 2017; Liu et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by previously published data from the authors' group (Liu et al., 2017; Liu et al., 2018).

claim: The methylated sidechain of arginine is located in a more open catalytic space containing negatively charged residues in JMJD6 compared to that of JMJD5.
source: However, the methylated sidechain of arginine is located in a more open catalytic space containing negatively charged residues, compared to that of JMJD5, indicating that the pocket could hold more than one sidechain (Figure 1A).
evidence: This claim is based on structural comparison between JMJD6 and JMJD5 crystal structures.

claim: The pocket in JMJD6 could hold more than one sidechain.
source: However, the methylated sidechain of arginine is located in a more open catalytic space containing negatively charged residues, compared to that of JMJD5, indicating that the pocket could hold more than one sidechain (Figure 1A).
evidence: This claim is inferred from the structural observation of the open catalytic space.

claim: JMJD6 may have a novel substrate recognition mode different from that of JMJD5.
source: This may suggest a novel substrate recognition mode, which is different from that of JMJD5 (Liu et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is speculative and based on structural comparison.

claim: JMJD6 binds to substrates with methylarginine or possibly methyllysine or both arginine and lysine with and without methylation.
source: First, JMJD6 does bind to substrates with methylarginine or possibly methyllysine or both arginine and lysine with and without methylation (Figure 1B,C).
evidence: This claim is based on the crystal structure showing binding to monomethylarginine.

claim: Peptides or proteins could be cognate substrates of JMJD6 instead of RNA or DNA.
source: Third, peptides or proteins could be cognate substrates instead of RNA or DNA, which do not contain any positive charge with or without methylation.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the structural observation that the binding pocket accommodates positively charged residues.

claim: The catalytic center of JMJD6 contains analogous residues present in JMJD5 and JMJD7.
source: Fourth, the catalytic center contains analogous residues present in JMJD5 and JMJD7, suggesting a similar novel catalytic mechanism as those of JMJD5 and JMJD7 through an imidic acid as proton mediator (Figure 1D; Lee et al., 2017; Liu et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is based on structural comparison and previously published data.

claim: JMJD6 has a similar novel catalytic mechanism as those of JMJD5 and JMJD7 through an imidic acid as proton mediator.
source: Fourth, the catalytic center contains analogous residues present in JMJD5 and JMJD7, suggesting a similar novel catalytic mechanism as those of JMJD5 and JMJD7 through an imidic acid as proton mediator (Figure 1D; Lee et al., 2017; Liu et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is inferred from structural similarity and previously published mechanistic studies.

claim: JMJD6 has activities on bulk histone in vitro.
source: Interestingly, JMJD6 does in fact have activities on bulk histone in vitro (Figure 2—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This claim is supported by in vitro assay data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1A.

claim: With or without Jmjd6, the level of arginine methylated histones or overall histone levels does not change in MEF cells in vivo.
source: Most importantly, with or without Jmjd6, the level of arginine methylated histones or overall histone levels does not change in MEF cells in vivo (Figure 2—figure supplement 1B), which is in stark contrast to those of JMJD5 and JMJD7 (Liu et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by Western blot data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1B.

claim: Histone tails are not cognate substrates of JMJD6.
source: These data suggest that histone tails are not cognate substrates of JMJD6.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the observation that histone levels do not change with or without Jmjd6 in vivo, despite in vitro activity.

claim: JMJD6 binds to LARP7 on 7SK snRNP.
source: Parenthetically, it is reported that JMJD6 binds to LARP7 on 7SK snRNP (Weimann et al., 2013)
evidence: This claim is supported by previously published data (Weimann et al., 2013).

claim: JMJD6 works on methyl cap of 5' 7SK snRNA.
source: works on methyl cap of 5' 7SK snRNA (Liu et al., 2013)
evidence: This claim is supported by previously published data (Liu et al., 2013).

claim: Binding affinities between JMJD6 and histone peptides with or without arginine methylation are weak and around ~150 μM.
source: From fluorescence polarization binding assays, binding affinities between JMJD6 and peptides are weak and around ~150 μM (Figure 3—figure supplement 1D,E).
evidence: This claim is supported by fluorescence polarization assay data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1D,E.

claim: The first 150 residues of MePCE contains 27 prolines, representing 18.0% prolines.
source: We expect that the ~25 kDa fragment from N-terminal of MePCE may contain 200 residues or less due to rich proline residues within the N-terminal of MePCE (first 150 residues of MePCE contains 27 prolines, 18.0% prolines).
evidence: This claim is based on sequence analysis of MePCE.

claim: The anti-MePCE antibody used was generated using a peptide immunogen containing residues 200–250 of MePCE.
source: The anti-MePCE antibody used in this assay was generated using a peptide immunogen containing residues 200–250 of MePCE.
evidence: This is a methodological detail about the antibody used.

claim: The ~65 kDa band detected by anti-MePCE antibody may correspond to the cleaved C-terminal segment of MePCE containing the approximate residues 200–689.
source: Thus, the ~65 kDa band may correspond to the cleaved C-terminal segment of MePCE containing the approximate residues 200–689.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the antibody epitope and the observed band size.

claim: Peptides of 81–160 and 187–244 of MePCE did not show any cleavage when incubated with JMJD6.
source: Peptides of 81–160 and 187–244 did not show any cleavage when incubated with JMJD6.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from peptide cleavage assays.

claim: Peptides of 154–184 of MePCE showed cleavage activity, but at levels of <1% compared to peptide input.
source: Peptides of 154–184 showed cleavage activity, but at levels of <1% compared to peptide input.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from peptide cleavage assays.

claim: The low activity of peptides 154–184 was attributed to insolubility and dimerization via C177 oxidation.
source: We attributed this low activity as a matter of insolubility and dimerization via C177 oxidation.
evidence: This claim is an inference to explain the low activity observed.

claim: The MePCE (161-179) R171-me2s/C177S peptide has a molecular weight of 2,290.57 Da.
source: The MePCE (161-179) peptide with symmetric dimethylation on R171 and C177S mutation has a molecular weight of 2,290.57 Da.
evidence: This is a calculated molecular weight based on the peptide sequence and modifications.

claim: After wild-type JMJD6 cleavage between R170 and R171 of MePCE peptide, the N-terminal product has a molecular weight of 1,243.48 Da and the C-terminal product has a molecular weight of 1,065.11 Da.
source: After wild-type JMJD6 cleavage between R170 and R171, the major peaks* (black triangles) with the molecular weight of 1,243.48 Da corresponds to the N-terminal product and the molecular weight of 1,065.11 Da corresponds to the C-terminal product respectively.
evidence: This claim is supported by mass spectrometry data shown in Figure 2E.

claim: Fluorescence polarization assays cross-validated the Kd values obtained via MST for JMJD6 binding to MePCE peptides.
source: Fluorescence polarization assays were used to cross-validate the Kd values obtained via MST above, all of which respectively fell within the margin of error (Figure 3—figure supplement 1A,B,C).
evidence: This claim is supported by fluorescence polarization assay data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1A,B,C.

claim: Methylation on R170 of MePCE diminishes binding to JMJD6 marginally.
source: These data suggest that methylation on R171 enhances binding nearly 3-fold compared to no modification, whereas methylation on R170 diminishes binding marginally.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the binding affinity measurements obtained via MST.

claim: No meaningful binding was observed between JMJD6 and C-peptide.
source: No meaningful binding was observed for the C-peptide (Figure 3F).
evidence: This claim is supported by MST assay data shown in Figure 3F, where C-peptide serves as a negative control.

claim: Wild-type MePCE with C-terminal His6 tag generates two bands when probed with anti-His6 antibody in MePCE KO 293T cells.
source: Interestingly, when probed with anti-His6 antibody in a western blot, wild-type MePCE generates two bands of MePCE (Figure 3I, left lane), consistent with Figure 2B
evidence: This claim is supported by Western blot data shown in Figure 3I.

claim: Mutant MePCE (R169A/R170A/R171A/R172A) with C-terminal His6 tag does not generate two bands when probed with anti-His6 antibody in MePCE KO 293T cells.
source: whereas the mutant version does not (Figure 3I, right lane), suggesting that this site is the authentic cleavage site for JMJD6.
evidence: This claim is supported by Western blot data shown in Figure 3I.

claim: Two major bands show up with wild-type MePCE when overexpressed in JMJD6 overexpressing MEF cells.
source: Once again consistent with Figure 2B, two major bands show up with the wild-type MePCE (Figure 3J, left lane)
evidence: This claim is supported by Western blot data shown in Figure 3J.

claim: Only one major band and one faint band show up with mutant MePCE when overexpressed in JMJD6 overexpressing MEF cells.
source: whereas only one major band and one faint band show up with the mutant MePCE (Figure 3J, right lane).
evidence: This claim is supported by Western blot data shown in Figure 3J.

claim: The native form of MePCE generates a small band in in vitro assay with JMJD6.
source: The native form of MePCE generates a small band (Figure 3—figure supplement 2B), consistent with Figure 2C
evidence: This claim is supported by in vitro assay data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 2B.

claim: The mutant MePCE does not generate any additional band in in vitro assay with JMJD6.
source: whereas the mutant MePCE does not generate any additional band (Figure 3—figure supplement 2C).
evidence: This claim is supported by in vitro assay data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 2C.

claim: JMJD6 is the cognate protease of MePCE and cleaves at the R171 site within MePCE.
source: Taken together, we propose that JMJD6 is the cognate protease of MePCE and cleaves at the R171 site within MePCE.
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple lines of experimental evidence including binding assays, cleavage assays, and mutagenesis studies.

claim: Cleavage of histone tails by JMJD5 and JMJD7 could lead to tailless nucleosomes, which are unstable and are more readily overcome by Pol II during transcription.
source: We previously reported that cleavage of histone tails by JMJD5 and JMJD7 could lead to tailless nucleosomes, which are unstable and are more readily overcome by Pol II during transcription (Liu et al., 2017; Liu et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by previously published data from the authors' group (Liu et al., 2017; Liu et al., 2018).

claim: JMJD6 assists BRD4 to recruit P-TEFb to Pol II CTD by disrupting the 7SK snRNP complex.
source: We propose that JMJD6 assists bromodomain containing 4 (BRD4) to recruit P-TEFb to Pol II CTD by disrupting the 7SK snRNP complex.
evidence: This is a proposed model based on the totality of experimental evidence presented in the manuscript.

claim: JMJD6 binds to 20–50 nt newly transcribed 5' prime end of ssRNAs of initiated Pol II of any stimulating genes.
source: JMJD6 binds to 20–50 nt newly transcribed 5' prime end of ssRNAs of initiated Pol II of any stimulating genes.
evidence: This claim is part of the proposed model and is based on previously published binding data.

claim: The association between BRD4 and JMJD6 allows BRD4 to bring P-TEFb (CDK9) to close proximity of CTD of Pol II, allowing for Ser2-CTD phosphorylation.
source: The association between BRD4 and JMJD6 allows BRD4 to bring P-TEFb (CDK9) to close proximity of CTD of Pol II, allowing for Ser2-CTD phosphorylation (Figure 4E).
evidence: This claim is part of the proposed model based on experimental evidence and published literature.

claim: The recruitment of P-TEFb by JMJD6, with the assistance of BRD4, is similar to that of TAT protein hijacking P-TEFb complex after associating with TAR transcript to trigger the expression of HIV retroviral genome.
source: Remarkably, this recruitment of P-TEFb by JMJD6, with the assistance of BRD4, is similar to that of TAT protein hijacking P-TEFb complex after associating with TAR transcript to trigger the expression of HIV retroviral genome (Figure 4F; Peterlin et al., 2012; Zhou et al., 2012; C Quaresma et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is an analogy drawn between the proposed mechanism and the known TAT/TAR mechanism, supported by citations.

claim: A species of Ser2p-CTD of Pol II is generated by CDK9.
source: This data suggests not only that JMJD6's cleavage of MePCE is essential for P-TEFb to be released from the 7SK snRNP complex and ultimately the phosphorylation of Ser2-CTD of Pol II, but also further cross-confirms that a species of Ser2p-CTD of Pol II is indeed generated by CDK9.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the experimental observations showing the relationship between JMJD6, MePCE, and Ser2p-CTD levels.

claim: JMJD6's cleavage of MePCE is essential for P-TEFb to be released from the 7SK snRNP complex and ultimately the phosphorylation of Ser2-CTD of Pol II.
source: This data suggests not only that JMJD6's cleavage of MePCE is essential for P-TEFb to be released from the 7SK snRNP complex and ultimately the phosphorylation of Ser2-CTD of Pol II
evidence: This claim is inferred from the totality of experimental evidence showing the effects of JMJD6 on MePCE and Ser2p-CTD levels.

claim: CDK9 interacts with the N-terminal region of MePCE (1-400).
source: Of interest, Shelton et al. (2018) showed that CDK9 interacts with the N-terminal region of MePCE (1-400)).
evidence: This claim is supported by previously published data (Shelton et al., 2018).

claim: There is a very similar JMJD6 cutting site around residues 363–367 (-RKRRR-) of MePCE compared to the site around residues 167–172 (-KRRRR-).
source: We found a very similar JMJD6 cutting site around residues 363–367 (-RKRRR-) compared the site we characterized around residues 167–172 (-KRRRR-).
evidence: This claim is based on sequence analysis identifying a similar motif.

claim: MePCE may act as an anchor site for CDK9 on 7SK snRNP complex.
source: If JMJD6 also cuts this site as well, it seems that MePCE may act as an anchor site for CDK9 on 7SK snRNP complex.
evidence: This is a speculative claim based on the identification of a second potential cleavage site.

claim: JMJD6 is critical for embryonic development.
source: The totality of our results is consistent with the critical role of JMJD6 in embryonic development, which is neonatal lethal without Jmjd6 (Li et al., 2003; Böse et al., 2004).
evidence: This claim is supported by previously published knockout studies (Li et al., 2003; Böse et al., 2004).

claim: Upon stimulation of cells, signals will reach specific transcription factors through signal transduction pathways.
source: First, upon stimulation of cells, signals will reach specific transcription factors through signal transduction pathways.
evidence: This is part of the proposed model based on established knowledge of signal transduction.

claim: Transcription factors recruit P300/CBP with the help of H3K4(me1) at enhancer regions.
source: These transcription factors will recruit P300/CBP with the help of H3K4(me1) at enhancer regions, which in turn acetylates H3 and/or H4 on the same nucleosome bound by P300/CBP through association with H3K4(me1) to generate acetylated H3 and/or H4 (Figure 5A).
evidence: This is part of the proposed model based on established knowledge of transcription regulation.

claim: P300/CBP acetylates H3 and/or H4 on the same nucleosome to generate acetylated H3 and/or H4.
source: These transcription factors will recruit P300/CBP with the help of H3K4(me1) at enhancer regions, which in turn acetylates H3 and/or H4 on the same nucleosome bound by P300/CBP through association with H3K4(me1) to generate acetylated H3 and/or H4 (Figure 5A).
evidence: This is part of the proposed model based on established knowledge of histone acetylation.

claim: BRD4 is recruited to acetylated H3 and/or H4.
source: Next, BRD4 is recruited to acetylated H3 and/or H4, and in turn engages with JMJD6 and the initiated Pol II complex.
evidence: This is part of the proposed model based on established knowledge of BRD4 function.

claim: BRD4 engages with JMJD6 and the initiated Pol II complex.
source: Next, BRD4 is recruited to acetylated H3 and/or H4, and in turn engages with JMJD6 and the initiated Pol II complex.
evidence: This is part of the proposed model based on experimental evidence and published literature.

claim: JMJD6 specifically cleaves MePCE of the 7SK snRNP complex to release the P-TEFb complex containing CDK9.
source: JMJD6 specifically cleaves MePCE of the 7SK snRNP complex so as to release the P-TEFb complex containing CDK9 (Figure 5B).
evidence: This is part of the proposed model based on experimental evidence presented in the manuscript.

claim: JMJD6 and BRD4 bring P-TEFb to close proximity of CTD of Pol II through super elongation complex.
source: Finally, JMJD6 and BRD4 brings P-TEFb to close proximity of CTD of Pol II through super elongation complex.
evidence: This is part of the proposed model based on experimental evidence and published literature.

claim: P-TEFb (CDK9) phosphorylates Ser2-CTD of Pol II.
source: P-TEFb (CDK9) then phosphorylates Ser2-CTD of Pol II (Figure 5C).
evidence: This is part of the proposed model based on established knowledge of P-TEFb function.

claim: The 7SK snRNP complex primarily functions to sequester the CDK9-containing P-TEFb until stimulation.
source: It is well established that the 7SK snRNP complex primarily functions to sequester the CDK9-containing P-TEFb until stimulation (Jang et al., 2005; Yang et al., 2005).
evidence: This claim is supported by previously published data (Jang et al., 2005; Yang et al., 2005).

claim: BRD4 is claimed to be responsible for the recruitment P-TEFb to the promoters of Pol II pausing regulated genes.
source: Compared to the efficient recruitment of P-TEFb (including CDK9 and Cyclin T1) by TAT protein in human immunodeficiency virus (HIV) (Peterlin et al., 2012), BRD4 is claimed to be responsible for the recruitment P-TEFb to the promoters of Pol II pausing regulated genes (Jang et al., 2005; Yang et al., 2005; C Quaresma et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by previously published data (Jang et al., 2005; Yang et al., 2005; C Quaresma et al., 2016).
